title: Pediatric Status Epilepticus — Treatment Ladder
keywords: the 2016 AES algorithm is a timed staircase, not a single drug choice — stabilization 0-5 minutes, first-line benzodiazepine 5-20 minutes, second-line agent 20-40 minutes, third-line 40-60 minutes
give a full benzodiazepine dose, not a timid partial dose, under-dosing is the most common preventable error
check glucose in the first few minutes, hypoglycemia is a reversible cause that a benzodiazepine alone won't fix
no line yet, don't wait for one, IM midazolam works and buys time to get access

if seizures continue past the second-line agent, this is refractory status epilepticus and needs intubation for a continuous infusion, not a third sequential bolus drug tried one after another indefinitely
sources: Glauser T, et al. Evidence-Based Guideline: Treatment of Convulsive Status Epilepticus in Children and Adults: Report of the Guideline Committee of the American Epilepsy Society. Epilepsy Curr. 2016;16(1):48-61.

changelog.change: Initial entry — a genuine content gap (Content audit 2026-09-15, fresh-look Batch 6). The individual second-line drug cards (fosphenytoin, levetiracetam, valproate, lorazepam, midazolam) already existed but nothing unified them into the timed algorithm, unlike the adult status-epilepticus-adult module which already has this structure.

purpose: The timed, staged treatment algorithm for pediatric convulsive status epilepticus — when to escalate, not just what each individual drug's dose is.
ageRange: Pediatric, all ages — dosing for each stage lives in the individual weight-based drug cards linked below.

body.text: Status epilepticus = a seizure lasting more than 5 minutes, OR two or more seizures without full recovery of consciousness between them. The core principle across every stage: give FULL doses promptly rather than partial/timid doses — under-dosing is one of the most common preventable errors, and benzodiazepines become progressively less effective the longer a seizure continues (GABA-A receptor internalization), which is exactly why the algorithm is time-staged rather than open-ended.

rows: Airway/breathing/circulation, oxygen, monitor, IV access if readily available (don't delay benzodiazepine for it), POINT-OF-CARE GLUCOSE — treat hypoglycemia immediately if found, since a benzodiazepine alone won't fix a hypoglycemic seizure.

A FULL-dose benzodiazepine — IV lorazepam if access is present; IM midazolam (or intranasal/buccal midazolam) if no IV access yet, rather than waiting to establish one. See the linked lorazepam/midazolam dosing cards for weight-based dosing. May repeat once if the first dose doesn't terminate the seizure within a few minutes.

If seizures continue despite an adequate benzodiazepine trial: levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, or valproate — choice depends on patient factors (e.g. valproate generally avoided with known/suspected hepatic or mitochondrial disease; fosphenytoin avoided in some cardiac conduction concerns) and institutional preference. See the linked individual dosing cards.

If seizures persist past an adequate second-line agent, this is REFRACTORY status epilepticus — the next step is typically a different second-line agent OR proceeding to intubation and a continuous infusion (midazolam, pentobarbital, or propofol infusion per institutional/ICU protocol), not an indefinite sequence of additional bolus drugs tried one after another.

body.text: Reaching the third-line/refractory stage means involving critical care and typically proceeding to a continuous infusion under controlled, monitored conditions (usually with intubation) — this is an escalation in the LEVEL of care, not just the next drug on a list.
In parallel with the drug ladder

items: Check glucose early and treat hypoglycemia immediately if found — this is a reversible cause the drug ladder alone won't address.

Look for and treat other reversible causes in parallel with drug treatment, not sequentially after it — fever/infection, electrolyte derangement (especially hyponatremia in young infants), toxic ingestion, known epilepsy with a missed anticonvulsant dose, trauma, or a known VP shunt malfunction.
Continuous or frequent reassessment of airway and breathing throughout — benzodiazepines and the second-line agents all carry some respiratory depression risk, especially when given in sequence.
